title: Cloud Computing: Concepts, Models, and Applications
topics: AI and Big Data in Cloud

bullets.text: Overview of lecture topics: meaning, importance, features, models, advantages, challenges, and applications.
Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet.
Services include servers, storage, databases, networking, software, analytics, and AI.
It's a way of renting computing resources instead of buying and maintaining them.
Analogy: paying for electricity consumed, not owning the power plant.
This model makes technology more affordable, scalable, and convenient.
On-demand self-service: users access resources instantly without human interaction.
Broad network access: services available over the internet from various devices.
Resource pooling: providers share resources across multiple customers with data isolation.
Rapid elasticity: resources can scale up or down quickly based on demand.
Measured service: usage is monitored and billed based on consumption.
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): Provider delivers fundamental computing resources (VMs, storage); users build applications. Example: Amazon Web Services EC2.
Platform as a Service (PaaS): Provider delivers infrastructure and a development platform; developers build apps without server management. Example: Google App Engine.
Software as a Service (SaaS): Provider delivers ready-to-use applications over the internet; users access via browser. Examples: Gmail, Microsoft 365, Zoom.
Public Cloud: Services delivered over the internet, shared by multiple organizations; cost-effective, scalable, but may raise security concerns.
Private Cloud: Dedicated to a single organization; offers more control and security, but can be more expensive.
Hybrid Cloud: Combines public and private clouds to balance flexibility with security.
Community Cloud: Shared by several organizations with common goals or requirements (e.g., healthcare, education).
Reduces costs: eliminates heavy investment in hardware, maintenance, or data centers.
Improves scalability: easily expand or reduce resources during peak/off-peak times.
Enhances flexibility: employees access applications and data from anywhere with internet.
Provides reliability: leading providers offer backup, disaster recovery, and high availability.
Supports innovation: faster experimentation and deployment without infrastructure limits.
Security and privacy: trusting providers to protect sensitive data on remote servers.
Downtime: internet connectivity issues can affect access to critical resources.
Compliance: adherence to strict industry regulations for data storage (e.g., healthcare, finance).
Vendor lock-in: difficulty and cost associated with switching cloud providers.
Performance concerns: potential issues for applications requiring high speed or low latency.
Data storage and backup (Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive).
Business collaboration (Slack, Microsoft Teams) and entertainment streaming (Netflix, Spotify).
Healthcare (electronic medical records, telemedicine) and education (Coursera, Google Classroom).
Research: large-scale data analysis, machine learning, and AI projects.
Cloud in AI and Big Data: renting high-performance computing for data processing and AI research.
Edge computing: processing data closer to source (IoT devices) to reduce latency, relies on cloud for management.
Multi-cloud strategies: using multiple providers to avoid vendor lock-in and improve reliability.
Serverless computing: developers focus on code, cloud provider automatically manages infrastructure.
Continued focus on security and compliance advancements.
Integration with AI, blockchain, and 5G to expand possibilities.
Summary: Cloud computing offers flexibility, scalability, and cost savings, with various models and applications.
